Q: On fresh Conda installation of PyProj: pyproj unable to set database path. _pyproj_global_context_initialize() A:

Yes, this is smelling like environment variables.

If you have PostgreSQL/PostGIS or QGIS installed, they often set a system-wide variable called PROJ_LIB or PROJ_DATA.

I'd rather not delete them if they have a value...

Since it's working, that's a win. Otherwise I'd force your specific conda to use its own data path:

# Set the correct path for your specific environment
conda env config vars set PROJ_LIB="C:\Users\YOUR_USER\Miniconda3\envs\geopandas\Library\share\proj"

# Deactivate and reactivate to apply (yes)
conda deactivate
conda activate geopandas

Q: How to get the records of last month in SQL Server? A:

Using this query you can get last month from current date:

select month(dateadd(month, -1, getdate())) as lastmonth;

By this query you can confirm if you are getting the last month or not. You will see number from 1 to 12 based on month.

Using this month logic i was able to retrieve last month data from my employees table.

See,

Select * from employees

Where month(hire_date) = month(dateadd(month, -1, getdate()));

This is just like we are subtracting numbers and its so simple to use now.

You can use

convert(date, getdate())

To get only the date in yyyy-mm-dd format.

Q: PolarDB PG partitioned table: a IN (...) AND b = const predicate not reduced per partition, causes many useless index probes — how to optimize? A:
  1. Is there a way to make PostgreSQL/PolarDB prune or reduce the IN (...) list per partition, so each partition only gets the values that fall into its range?

Postgres partition pruning means it'll avoid scanning mismatched partitions entirely. A in (A,B,C) makes no sense for partition holding only D, but that partition gets pruned so there's no need to reduce that to an A in (), a false, to skip it - it's already being skipped.

If you fear A in (A,B,C) isn't optimal on A partition and you'd like that to be reduced to A in (A), with B and C removed in accordance with the partition key - I agree. I'd take this even further and throw that whole condition away entirely when scanning individual partitions, since it's been verified earlier and evaluated to true - otherwise the partition would get pruned away.

I wouldn't be surprised if this feature was already in there. Notice that the explain plan only shows the effect of this (pruning doesn't show up as an actual step in the plan), and it kind of makes sense to leave the superfluous condition in the index scan so that it doesn't seem just ignored and discarded. Still, re-evaluating it at that stage would contribute nothing.

Here, you can see the third partition getting pruned away, and only the first two get a scan:
demo at db<>fiddle

create table my_parted_table(a int,b int,primary key(a,b)) partition by range(a,b);
create table p1_100 partition of my_parted_table for values from (1,0) to (1,1001);
create table p2_100 partition of my_parted_table for values from (2,0) to (2,1001);
create table p3_100 partition of my_parted_table for values from (3,0) to (3,1001);

insert into my_parted_table
select a,b
from generate_series(1,3)as generated1(a)
cross join generate_series(1,1000)as generated2(b);

analyze my_parted_table;

explain analyze verbose
SELECT *
FROM my_parted_table
WHERE a IN (1,2)
  AND b=9;
